source.title: Why Better Cross-Lingual Alignment Fails for Better Cross-Lingual Transfer: Case of Encoders
source.authors: Yana Veitsman; Yihong Liu; Hinrich Schütze

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether cross-lingual alignment measurements track downstream outcomes and reports that their relationship depends on alignment configuration and representation level. Its alignment measurements also vary across layers and language-pair groups, bearing on V6; it does not test convergence with model scale or across modalities.
record.gate_note: The study explicitly aligns XLM-R models and measures cross-lingual embedding distances, cosine similarities, and retrieval, so those outcomes are included. Downstream accuracy and gradient-similarity results are omitted because they do not themselves measure representational convergence. The paper reports no scale sweep or cross-modal comparison.
record.test_reason: The study trains one model, XLM-R base (270M), to bring its own representations of different languages closer, using an explicit contrastive alignment objective. It then measures whether those induced changes predict downstream transfer. No version is about this. It does not compare independently trained models (V1, V3), vision and language models (V2), mappings between models (V4), or recurring features across models (V5). Its sensitivity results concern within-model cross-lingual similarity that the authors induced on purpose, not measured convergence between models (V6, V7). Under the gate rules (behaviour induced deliberately; a related but different construct), it does not test the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that improved cross-lingual representational alignment does not reliably improve downstream transfer, and that alignment should be treated as a diagnostic property rather than a task-independent proxy. They argue that compatibility between the alignment and downstream objectives (via gradient similarity) explains the gap. They also find that linear-only fine-tuning preserves alignment benefits better than full fine-tuning.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a modified hierarchical contrastive alignment objective on XLM-R and measures cross-lingual embedding distances and retrieval. It is not a reproduction of either cited convergence study’s method.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported alignment patterns vary with representation layer, alignment loss configuration, and language-pair group. The paper also compares cosine-based measures with sentence retrieval, which it says show the same tendency.

fits_no_version.finding: Explicit contrastive alignment of XLM-R base raises cross-lingual cosine similarity slightly (mostly about +.01) and raises retrieval (up to about +0.09 R@5) under sentence-level losses. Token-only alignment (S0T1M0) sharply lowers retrieval (as much as −0.67 R@5). These changes do not predict downstream POS-tagging or sentence-classification transfer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Induced cross-lingual alignment within a multilingual encoder, measured by embedding similarity or retrieval, does not reliably predict downstream cross-lingual transfer, and its direction depends on the alignment loss.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 6th Workshop on Multilingual Representation Learning (MRL 2026)
record.problems: The analysis uses a single 270M encoder model and one contrastive alignment objective. The paper notes that it does not examine pretraining language distributions, data quality or volume, or tokenization disparities. Some layer-wise results are presented in figures, and the text does not give their exact numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: Downstream POS-tagging and sentence-classification accuracy, and gradient similarities, were not included because they do not directly measure convergence. Detailed per-language-pair and per-configuration values in Appendix Tables 5, 6, and 8 were not extracted exhaustively; the rows retain the text’s stated aggregate patterns and key conditions.

untested.parts: No scale sweep and no comparison of independently trained models.
No vision-language or paired image-caption data.
No comparison across seeds or initializations.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation test between models.
No feature or circuit universality test.
Metric and data dependence of convergence between models is not tested. The study measures only induced cross-lingual similarity within one model.
No test of plateauing, or of shared data or objectives as causes of convergence between models.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T5' for V6 is rejected. V6 concerns how measured convergence between models depends on the metric and inputs. This paper measures cross-lingual similarity within a single model after training it on purpose to produce that similarity. The reader also mislabelled a V6 'supports' and a V6 'limits_scope' verdict; both are removed.

versions.untested_parts: No model-scale or capability sweep, nor comparison of independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, or data.
No paired image-caption representations or vision-language comparison.
No comparison of models trained from different initializations for shared features or subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test.
No recurring interpretable features or circuits are tested.

The study varies alignment loss, layer, and language-pair/input group, and compares embedding-based measurements with retrieval. It does not test OOD inputs or the effect of settings such as number of neighbours.
The study does not test whether convergence plateaus or whether shared pretraining data or objectives explain convergence.

rows.subject: XLM-Rbase (aligned variants; aggregate across models and languages)
rows.stage_stated: alignment fine-tuned; also evaluated after downstream fine-tuning
rows.operation_detail: Measured changes in token- and sentence-level cosine embedding distances from XLM-Rbase across layers and alignment configurations.

conditions.value: Across tested configurations; exception noted for S0T1M0
Cross-language pairs; token and sentence representations

rows.measure: Change in cosine-based embedding distance from XLM-Rbase
rows.value: Distances generally decrease in the 8th layer for aligned and downstream fine-tuned models, except under S0T1M0.
rows.note: The reported pattern varies with loss configuration and layer; lower and final layers are described as more heterogeneous.
rows.check: Measures within-model cross-lingual distance after deliberate contrastive alignment fine-tuning, not convergence between models. Not linked to V6.

rows.subject: XLM-Rbase (aligned variants; aggregate across models and languages)
rows.operation_detail: Measured token- and sentence-level cosine embedding distances from XLM-Rbase under token-only alignment.
rows.value: The general decrease in distances at the 8th layer is reported to have an exception under S0T1M0; the direction and magnitude for this exception are not stated in the text.
rows.note: The text identifies this configuration as an exception but does not state whether distance increased or stayed unchanged.
rows.check: Same construct problem as r1. For S0T1M0, Tables 5 and 8 show retrieval drops (R@5 down to −0.67 for kaz-eng) and small cosine decreases (−.01 to −.03). The distance direction in Figure 3 still can't be read from the text.

rows.subject: XLM-Rbase (aligned variants; aggregate across language pairs)
rows.operation_detail: Measured sentence-level cosine similarity changes from XLM-Rbase.

conditions.value: Sentence pairs from FLORES-200; language-pair results vary

rows.baseline: XLM-Rbase; Spanish–English baseline similarity is approximately .98.
rows.value: Gains are generally modest; most improvements remain below .02. Spanish–English reaches approximately .98.
rows.note: The reported gains are small and vary by language pair and alignment configuration.
rows.check: Construct problem as r1. Most gains are about +.01 in Table 8; S0T1M0 gives small decreases. The .98 figure is the Spanish–English similarity, not a baseline for all pairs.

rows.subject: XLM-Rbase (aligned variants; aggregate over the stated language group)
rows.operation_detail: Measured sentence-level cosine similarity changes from XLM-Rbase for non-aligned language pairs involving English and different scripts.
rows.value: The smallest gains are observed for this group; the text suggests alignment fine-tuning may partially shift these languages away from the English-centered representational space.
rows.note: The paper describes this group comparatively; no group-level numerical gain is stated in the text.
rows.check: Construct problem as r1. Table 8 gives Group 3 values of about +.01 for most configurations and −.02 to +.01 under S0T1M0.

rows.subject: XLM-Rbase (aligned variants; aggregate reported in the retrieval tables)
rows.operation_detail: Measured sentence retrieval changes from XLM-Rbase using R@5 and R@10.
rows.measure: Sentence retrieval R@5 and R@10 change
rows.value: Retrieval results exhibit the same tendency as sentence-level cosine similarity; the text does not state a summary numerical change.
rows.note: The paper presents retrieval as corroborating the cosine-similarity tendency, rather than reporting a disagreement between these measures.
rows.check: Construct problem as r1. The values are readable in Tables 5 and 6: sentence-loss configurations gain up to about +0.09 R@5. S0T1M0 causes large drops (−0.06 to −0.67), which is more than the 'same tendency' summary conveys.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Tested layers, alignment configurations, and language-pair groups
reader_labels.reason: The reported distance and cosine-similarity patterns vary by layer, loss configuration, and language-pair group, including an exception for S0T1M0 and particularly small gains for Group 3 (r1–r4).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Comparison of sentence cosine similarity and retrieval in the reported settings
reader_labels.reason: Retrieval is described as showing the same tendency as sentence-level cosine similarity, so these results do not show that the trend vanishes under the alternative measure; OOD inputs and neighbour-count settings were not tested (r3, r5).
